title: Abram Rescues Lot and Meets Melchizedek
summary: Four kings from the east, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, crush a rebellion by five kings of the Jordan plain, plunder Sodom and Gomorrah, and carry off Lot. Abram gathers 318 trained men from his household, pursues the invaders north past Dan, defeats them by night, and brings back Lot, the people, and the goods. On his return Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. Abram then refuses to keep any of Sodom's goods, so that no one can say the king of Sodom made him rich.
story: Lot chose the rich plain near Sodom in chapter 13, and this chapter shows where that choice led: into the path of a foreign army and into captivity. Abram, who had given Lot first choice, now risks his own life to rescue him. The chapter reveals a new side of Abram. He is no longer only a wandering herdsman but a man of standing, with trained men and allies, who can defeat kings. Yet the heart of the chapter is not the battle but two meetings afterward. One king, Melchizedek, blesses Abram in the name of God Most High; the other, the king of Sodom, offers him wealth. Abram receives the first and refuses the second, and the next chapter opens with God telling him, Do not be afraid, I am your shield and your very great reward.
historical:
This chapter reads differently from the stories around it. It names kings, alliances, years of tribute, and a military route, much like an ancient annal. None of the four eastern kings can be identified with a known ruler. Earlier scholars once equated Amraphel with Hammurabi of Babylon, a view now generally abandoned. Some of the names fit their regions: Chedorlaomer resembles Elamite royal names that begin with Kudur, and Tidal resembles the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya. Elam, in southwestern Iran, was at times a major power in Mesopotamian affairs in the early second millennium BC, but no campaign like this one is recorded outside Genesis. Scholars are divided: some regard the chapter as a late literary creation, while others see an old source behind it, pointing to its archaic names and to its explanatory notes updating old place names for later readers (Bela, that is, Zoar; the Valley of Siddim, that is, the Salt Sea; En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh). The mention of Dan (verse 14) is one such update, since the city received that name only in the time of the judges (Judges 18:29).

The invaders' route runs down the highlands east of the Jordan, through territories later known as Bashan, Moab, and Edom (Mount Seir), then south into the desert, back north through Kadesh and the Amalekite country, and on to Hazazon-tamar, identified elsewhere with En-gedi on the Dead Sea (2 Chronicles 20:2). The peoples they defeat, such as the Rephaim, Emim, and Horites, are remembered in Deuteronomy 2 as early inhabitants of those lands. The Dead Sea region was known in ancient times for its deposits of bitumen, the tar pits into which the fleeing kings fall.
cultural:
Small city-states in the ancient Near East often paid tribute to a distant overlord and rebelled when they thought they could. Punitive campaigns, plunder, and the capture of people as slaves were ordinary features of such wars. Abram's household of 318 trained men shows that he was a powerful chief, and his alliance with the Amorites Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner (bound by treaty, literally masters of a covenant) shows him taking his place among the local leaders. Night attacks and divided forces were classic tactics for a smaller force against a larger one.

Melchizedek's name means my king is righteousness, or king of righteousness, and Salem is almost certainly Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2 pairs Salem with Zion). A later king of Jerusalem bore a similar name, Adoni-zedek (Joshua 10:1). In the ancient world kings often served as priests, and El Elyon, God Most High, was a title for the supreme God known in West Semitic religion. Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils, a customary gift to a king or sanctuary, and then, raising his hand in the gesture of an oath, identifies God Most High with the LORD. By refusing even a thread or a sandal strap from the king of Sodom, he makes sure his wealth cannot be credited to a corrupt city, a sharp contrast with the gifts he accepted from Pharaoh in chapter 12.
literary: The chapter has three movements: a war report (verses 1 to 12), a rescue (verses 13 to 16), and two encounters (verses 17 to 24). The war report is dense with names and uses the formal style of royal records. The rescue is quick and decisive. The encounters are the theological center. The king of Sodom comes out to meet Abram in verse 17, but before he can speak, Melchizedek steps in (verses 18 to 20), so that the story sets the two kings side by side. Melchizedek gives (bread and wine, and a blessing); the king of Sodom bargains (give me the people, take the goods). Melchizedek's blessing is a short poem in two parallel lines, blessing Abram by God Most High and blessing God Most High for the victory. Abram's reply to the king of Sodom repeats Melchizedek's title for God word for word, showing where his allegiance lies. The chapter also contains the first use of the word Hebrew in the Bible, as outsiders might name Abram.

outline.t: Four kings of the east against five kings of the plain
Battle in the Valley of Siddim and Lot's capture
Abram pursues the invaders and rescues Lot
Melchizedek blesses Abram, and Abram gives a tenth
Abram refuses the king of Sodom's goods

doctrines.note: Melchizedek's blessing names God as God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, and credits him with delivering Abram's enemies into his hand. Behind the wars of kings stands the one God who owns heaven and earth. Abram's victory is God's work, and Abram acknowledges it with his tithe.

Melchizedek, a king who is also a priest, appears without introduction or genealogy and disappears again. Psalm 110 promises a royal figure who will be a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, and Hebrews applies that promise to Jesus, the King who is also the great High Priest.

Abram refuses wealth from the king of Sodom so that no one can say anyone but God made him rich. Faith shows itself in what a person will not take as well as in what he will risk. Having given Lot the best land and risked his life to save him, Abram trusts God alone to provide.

words.note: Kohen, priest. This is the first time the word appears in the Bible, and it describes not an Israelite but Melchizedek, a Canaanite king who serves God Most High. A priest stood between God and people, offering sacrifices and pronouncing blessings. Israel's priesthood will come later through Aaron; Melchizedek's is older and of a different kind.

Elyon, Most High. It is used as a title for God throughout the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, where it stresses his supremacy over all nations and powers. In other West Semitic religions a similar title was used for the high god. Abram claims it for the LORD in verse 22, declaring that the God Melchizedek serves under this title is the God who called him.

Ivri, Hebrew. This is its first use in the Bible. It is often connected with Eber, Abram's ancestor (10:21), or with a root meaning to cross over, describing someone from beyond the river. Some scholars have compared it with the term habiru, used in second-millennium texts for displaced people and mercenaries, though the link is debated. In the Old Testament it is often used by or about foreigners.

Maaser, a tenth or tithe. Giving a tenth of produce or plunder to a king or a god was a known practice in the ancient world. Abram's gift acknowledges Melchizedek's priestly authority and God's hand in the victory. Israel's later law formalized the tithe, and Hebrews 7 builds an argument on this very gift.

christ: Melchizedek is mentioned only once more in the Old Testament, but that mention is momentous. In Psalm 110, a royal psalm, God swears to the king, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). The New Testament quotes the first verse of that psalm about Christ more often than any other Old Testament verse, and the letter to the Hebrews devotes chapters 5 to 7 to its fourth verse. Hebrews notes that Melchizedek's name means “king of righteousness” and that king of Salem means king of peace (Hebrews 7:2). It draws meaning from the silence of Genesis about his parents and his death: “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (Hebrews 7:3). Because Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, Hebrews argues that Melchizedek was greater than Abraham and his descendant Levi, and so Christ's priesthood, in Melchizedek's order, surpasses the priesthood of the Law. Christ is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16). Some early Christian writers also saw in the bread and wine a foreshadowing of the Lord's Supper, a connection the New Testament itself does not make.

hard.a:
Genesis gives only three verses, and readers have filled the silence in different ways. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take him as a real Canaanite king of Jerusalem who worshiped the true God under the title God Most High, a sign that knowledge of God had not entirely disappeared outside Abram's family. Some ancient Jewish interpreters identified him with Shem, Noah's son, who on the figures of chapter 11 would still have been alive. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a text known as 11QMelchizedek pictures him as a heavenly figure who brings liberation and judgment at the end of days. Some Christians have taken him to be an appearance of the Son of God before the incarnation, reading Hebrews 7:3 literally.

Hebrews, however, says that Melchizedek is like the Son of God (the Greek suggests being made to resemble him), which points to a pattern rather than an identity. Its argument works because Genesis introduces him without ancestry and never records his death, so he can stand as a figure of a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end. On the most common reading, the point is not that Melchizedek was mysterious in himself, but that the way Scripture presents him points beyond him to Christ, the true King of righteousness and peace and a priest forever.

questions: Abram risked everything to rescue a relative whose own choices had put him in danger. Who in your life needs rescue, and what might it cost you to help?
Abram accepted blessing from Melchizedek but refused wealth from the king of Sodom. How do you decide which offers of help or gain you should accept and which you should turn down?
Abram gave a tenth of the spoils as an acknowledgment that God had given the victory. How do your giving and your gratitude reflect who you believe provides for you?
